The group was cycled in and out of various domains at random, never knowing which one would line them up properly. The few that did manage to find Wesker only had the barest of outlines. Get in, take him down, get the cuff off, scatter before he could get back up. He was NOT making it easy for them, however. Every time they got close, he would fight like a man possessed. The lack of coordination or patterns to his movement were almost impossible to plan around. The inability to tell who they would enter a trial with made personalized coordinated movements a joke. The best they could do was settle on roles in the moment — gestures, glances, short stolen moments of whispered agreements passed on the fly as they adjusted their approach a little tighter each time. It was far from perfect, but each trial got them closer. Each attempt injured them less and wore him down more. It was only a matter of time. The Fog cleared from the halls of Lery’s, Gabriel turning to check who his companions would be this round. Nea. Jake. Dwight. Each with a determined focus as they exchanged looks and scattered down separate halls. Generators were worked on with nervous glances around, hoping to at least ensure their eventual escape whether they managed their goal or not. It wouldn’t take them long to find him; their movements through the building were more strategic searches than the usual creeping attempts to stay hidden. Rather than scouting the best routes to generators, it became a basic path of quick moving glances into empty rooms that never really changed from one trial to another, and rapid fiddling with whatever machinery they tripped over in the process. The same wide corridors with their glass windows like observation tanks, the same antiseptic stink clinging to the drains. Glance, confirm a lack of their target, move on. Wesker’s presence was dimmed from it’s usual screaming radius that stretched half the building. The usual pounding of the survivor’s heart whenever the killer was even remotely close was barely noticeable in the moment — possibly drowned out by the anxiety that comes with knowing they’re about to do something monumentally stupid, but even without their scheming, his entire presence felt exhausted somehow. He was stalking the outer wall, glancing up at the edges of vents with clear distrust, his pace looking very much like predatory control. But the way Wesker stumbled — barely caught himself — then squared up with a snarl, shifting his grip on his hunting knife as he picked up his pace, it was clear that he was running on fumes. A half-blink that lagged a fraction behind the glance, a footfall that landed a little too hard, the shoulder working against a knot that wouldn’t release. A glaze to his eyes that made him look like he barely registered the halls around him, let alone their presence as they stalked at a distance. Yet somehow still moving. Still lethal. Still fast enough. Gabriel saw it and tilted his head the barest degree. Nea caught the signal. Dwight swallowed hard and nodded. Jake flexed his fingers once and let the breath out through his nose. This was such a stupid idea. Alright. Let’s try this again, then. It wasn’t clean. It couldn’t be. Nea showed herself first, bold and bright as bait, vaulting a window that offered only the illusion of safety. Wesker followed on instinct, knife coming up in a clean line that clipped air where she’d been a second before. The cuff gave a small, satisfied pulse, as if pleased to be consulted again after so much idle time. Dwight slid in quiet and knocked a hook out of commission with a practiced twist — better safe than sorry — then let himself be seen and lured their hunter toward a narrower corridor near the second ring. Jake came late, angling to brush Wesker’s shoulder and steal a step, not enough to commit, just enough to irritate. Gabriel shaped the angles, never leading, only appearing where the path wanted to narrow. Every second they kept him reacting gave the others time to set up. Dwight passed Nea a nod. Jake vanished into the shadows, doubling back. They didn’t speak. They couldn’t. Every time Wesker turned for the clear option, someone else was there — low, quick, moving with the kind of confidence that said they already knew the outcome. The cuff registered chaos and tried to punish him for it. A flash under the skin, an ache through the fingers, a tremor that was almost nothing until he needed that exact muscle to hold a grip. He shook his head hard enough to send stars across his vision and, in answer, found his knife hand a breath slow. He pushed through it. The next corner fractured. The next step slipped. Whatever margin he’d been operating on was narrowing by the stride. The only sounds were boots on tile, rasped breathing, and the hiss of the cuff as it built another spark. Wesker twitched and snarled, but he wasn’t coherent; his movements broke down under their own weight. One leg dragged. His off-hand flinched mid-swing. They drove him past the old admin desk and into the corridor that cut the complex in two. The walls there held a ghost of earlier noise — his own, if he’d been able to hear it. He recognized the corridor without recognizing the memory, almost instinctively trying to navigate away from it. He lunged for Dwight, expecting the man to crumple, not anticipating him leaning into the attack instead.
